I’m in Germany, so I can’t go back to China to hear one, or get one sent over :(


Alibaba’s Genie acoustics team and Boston Acoustics have described their collaboration as an attempt at integrated tuning within a “smart acoustics” framework. It’s the first time a Chinese manufacturer has put forward a concept like this and explained a complete system behind it. That’s why I wrote an article on smart acoustics last week. I won’t repeat the technical details here; you can read them in my article:

A history of acoustics: smart acoustics


Here I just want to talk about the background of smart acoustics and smart speakers and where they’re heading.


“Smart acoustics” is not yet a recognized term for a branch of acoustics. It may be easier to understand if you split it into “smart” and “acoustics.” So, roughly speaking, my definition is that smart acoustics is the umbrella term for the acoustic technologies involved in the smart home. Within a smart acoustics framework, these technologies are deeply integrated to improve the user experience.


The smart home (home automation) is the idea of bringing intelligent information technology into the home to improve the quality of domestic life. The smart home market was worth nearly $65 billion in 2020 and is projected to reach $163 billion by 2028 [1]. Smart speakers are one part of the smart home, and through both voice interaction and recognition and the audio technologies that improve listening, they play an increasingly important role in it.


How smart acoustics developed

The most important acoustic device in the smart home is probably the smart speaker. In 2022 the smart speaker market was worth $6.6 billion, more than 10% of the smart home market. In the age of smart devices, a speaker no longer just plays songs: it is an intelligent device combining multiple sensors, AI, and voice and acoustic algorithms, among other cutting-edge technologies.



You could say the smart speaker began with the launch of the Amazon Echo in 2014. Its AI core, Alexa, could understand users’ commands and play songs. From then on, smart speakers took the market by storm and gradually became the hub of the smart home. Beyond playing music, they gradually expanded into other parts of domestic life: you can ask about the weather, the stock market, travel plans or store opening hours, shop online or ask about all sorts of general topics. Smart speakers can also control lighting and air conditioning, set timers and alarms, and so on. They have found their way into every corner of home life.



Besides the Echo, the relatively successful makers outside China include Google, Sonos, Apple and HARMAN; in China, the main players are Baidu, Xiaomi, Huawei and Alibaba. According to reports in AI media such as QbitAI and Leiphone, Alibaba’s Genie Acoustics Lab has identified four trends in smart acoustics:


What’s interesting in this overall assessment is the part about music genres and acoustic architecture, where the team seems to be pursuing some consumer-oriented technical explorations of its own. Their future products and technology are worth watching. At the level of underlying technology, the adaptive, environment-aware drivers they propose are a promising direction.


With so many contenders vying for the crown, what secret techniques does each champion have up its sleeve? Let’s look at what I consider the most important technologies in smart acoustics.


The whole smart-acoustics interaction starts at the user’s mouth and ends at the user’s ear. The user speaks a command; thanks to source localization and noise reduction, the smart speaker’s microphone array hears it clearly. The speaker’s processor then runs a chain of processing to perform the various recognition functions and the tuning, and sends the reply or the music through the loudspeakers to the listener’s ears. The music can also be processed with 3D or spatial audio to add a sense of space and improve the listening experience.


As I said, the specific technologies involved are described in detail in this article:

A history of acoustics: smart acoustics

Where smart acoustics is heading

Smart acoustics is built on the smart speaker, so we certainly can’t ignore what a speaker is for in the first place: playing music. As we develop the technology, we have to keep a close eye on the human listening experience. Here, briefly, are the future trends in smart speaker audio that come to my mind.


3D audio

This isn’t exclusive to smart speakers; it’s a universal speaker technology. Once you have at least one smart speaker at home, 3D audio comes into play. Sitting on the sofa listening to a Jay Chou concert, for example, we can feel as though we’re actually there. Here’s the simplest example of 3D audio: we’re on the sofa, and Jay is singing on the stage right in front of us. He walks to the left of the stage to interact with the audience, and what we hear should match what we see; with our eyes closed, we’d still know he’s moved to the left of the stage. I wrote an article earlier describing in detail the 3D audio technology being developed at Facebook’s (now Meta’s) Reality Labs:

Hearing the future: audio in the life to come


Dr. Li, one of the authors in our group, worked with the people leading 3D audio at Facebook Reality Labs while doing research there.


Multi-room audio

This one is easy to grasp. We’re listening to music on a smart speaker in the living room and now want to go and spend some time in the bedroom. The most obvious thing to do is carry the speaker to the bedroom. But here’s the catch: with several smart speakers, that becomes tricky. So the next evolution of 3D audio is multi-room 3D audio. Put smart speakers in every room, track the listener’s position with sensors and render 3D audio in real time without spoiling the listening experience. Say you lie in the bedroom listening to music for a while, then get up to cook: the music follows you all the way to the kitchen and keeps playing while you cook. It’s not only about listening, either. With this setup you can call your voice assistant at any moment, instead of craning your neck and yelling at the room next door.


Personal sound zones

Two people on a sofa: one is listening to a concert, the other to an MIT open course, and neither hears the other’s audio. Pretty cool, right? Beyond the home, the technology is also a hot research topic for car cabins. It still has many limitations. In reverberant spaces, for example, multi-zone control is very hard to achieve, and performance varies across frequency ranges: it works better at low frequencies than at high frequencies, because high frequencies require a very large number of loudspeakers [2]. MEMS speakers could solve this problem, since they’re small and cheap. MEMS speakers are a cutting-edge area of acoustics in their own right and one of the technologies smart speakers could develop. Dr. Xiaoyu Niu, one of the authors in our group, works at the UT Acoustic MEMS Lab at the University of Texas, which has long focused on this research. If you’re interested, take a look at Dr. Niu’s article on directional MEMS microphones:

The most advanced microphone on Earth is… a fly’s ear


Nonlinear equalization

When we tune with EQ, we’re correcting not only the distortion caused by room reflections but also the linear and nonlinear distortion caused by the loudspeaker and amplification system. The equalization and tuning we usually talk about mainly address linear distortion. In recent years, some research has used Volterra filters to model the amplifier–driver–enclosure system before the signal is played, so as to equalize both the linear and the nonlinear distortion of the system.


Personalized tuning

Tuning tailored to the musical styles the user likes: the system learns the user’s preferences from the frequency content of the music they listen to, builds an equalization curve unique to that user and applies it to the music they play.


Directional sound

True wireless earbuds are great, but even the most comfortable earbuds become uncomfortable if you wear them long enough. So companies in China and abroad have started developing directional sound technology. An Israeli friend who shared my office during my PhD was working on exactly this a few years ago; they also call it “virtual headphones.” In China, as far as I know, the Institute of Acoustics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences is working on it too.


The idea is to merge headphones, loudspeakers and 3D reproduction into one, keeping the best of each and discarding the rest. It rests on three main principles:

  1. A 3D sensor identifies the position of the head, and especially of the two ears.
  2. Highly directional sound is aimed at the ears. Once the ear positions are known, the binaural audio signals are modulated onto ultrasound, so they can be delivered precisely to each ear. Some nonlinear, self-demodulating algorithm (I don’t know which; if you do, please enlighten me) then recovers the original audio at the ears.
  3. The ultrasound is emitted by a special loudspeaker, a multi-cell speaker module.




You wear nothing at all, yet get the effect of headphones. And it can do things a loudspeaker can’t: virtual headphones can make sound audible only to the target listener and to nobody else. That matters enormously in public spaces. Different areas of one museum room could play different audio for different themes without interfering with each other; a family of three in a car could each listen to their own music without headphones; you could take calls in an open office.



The concept is very appealing, though I don’t know how well it actually works. I’m curious how they solve several problems: how accurate the ear tracking is; whether ultrasound can really deliver the sound right to the entrance of the ear canal; how errors in the delivery position and the tracking throw off the HRTFs and degrade the binaural experience; and how they keep the demodulated sound from spreading into the surroundings.


Beyond algorithms, smart speakers are also returning to basics. They are no longer just made to be trendy “influencer” products, and some classic speaker architectures are back in product lineups. Hardware is another future trend for smart speakers: drivers made from innovative materials, such as ultrathin or flexible transducers, and new sensors.



That was a long digression, so here’s a divider, and now my actual answer to the question:


Since Amazon launched the Echo, more and more manufacturers have entered this field and released smart speaker after smart speaker. The blue ocean of a growing market has turned into the red ocean of a saturated one, and margins keep shrinking. To raise profits, companies have to move upmarket, which means making their products more competitive and strengthening their R&D capabilities, especially in the acoustic technologies described above. Many companies have already set up, or are setting up, dedicated acoustic R&D teams to sharpen their edge.


As for the Genie Acoustics Lab I mentioned, media reports say its latest experiments include using millimeter-wave radar to detect a person’s position, breathing, heartbeat, sleep and other states at a distance, merging smart acoustics with data about the human body.


To solve the problem of voice interaction when the speaker is playing loudly, they have also developed a “cat-ear algorithm.” The idea is that, like a cat, the speaker can hear voices from every direction and react just as sensitively: even when it’s playing music at full volume, the user can wake it easily by speaking at a normal level. The cat-ear algorithm has three parts, which are also the three pain points of voice interaction: echo cancellation, source localization and noise reduction.


Conventional echo cancellation relies mainly on linear filters to remove the speaker’s own linear echo. Tmall Genie adds an NAC module on top of this, which uses deep learning to cancel the speaker’s nonlinear echo. It exploits the differences between speech and non-speech sounds to deal with the nonlinear echo.


To sum up, smart acoustics can add real value to the consumer experience, and if it can be better combined with “traditional, classic” acoustics, especially through deep integration in physics, materials and manufacturing, there is much to look forward to. Boston Acoustics was founded in 1979 and now belongs to the same parent company as the high-end speaker brand B&W, but it focuses on B2B solutions. It has spent many years in home-theater and car speakers, has deep experience in loudspeaker acoustic design, and has supplied mature premium audio solutions to brands such as Jeep and the Chevrolet Camaro (the “Bumblebee” car from Transformers). What tuning solution they bring to this collaboration with Tmall Genie, and how it ultimately performs, remains to be tested by the product itself.
